body: Before ideals emerge, one deals with a bunch of refusals, or maybe it is the same coin after all. Going back to the Middle Ages and looking at the Kahn Madonna icon, we can see that something is off…
closing: Follow the blue lines marking the rear upright posts of the throne, from finial to base. Both posts lean toward the left and do not slant toward each other.
The orange lines mark the front upright posts and their tilt matches the rear posts. Both front and back pairs slant in parallel and do not converge.

Following the purple dashed lines marking the crosspieces joining rear and front uprights at seat level, these two lines slant downward to the right, and if one were to extend them, they would not meet in front of the panel.
The throne's foot supports are marked by the magenta lines, and both lines slant downward from left to right.
The green lines mark the footstool's foot supports, rear foot to front foot. The pattern matches the throne feet, and again both lines slant downward to the right.
The yellow line marks the visible front edge of the footstool's top surface, and teal lines mark the visible portions of the footstool's side edges, traced only as far as the drapery allows.

Stitching everything together, none of these five lines share a common root. They are constructed part by part, each with a consistent internal slant but no coordination across parts. This absence of a single controlling perspective, replaced by several local and mutually inconsistent ones, is what polycentric perspective means.

There has been a long debate about whether the absence of a central perspective point gives the illusion of the observer feeling watched by the painting, since the viewer has no point to fixate on. Another debate is whether there was some purpose behind the artistic style, or whether it is a lack of understanding of correct geometric representation.

Leaning in personally, it would be really arrogant and ignorant to assume that the understanding of perspective came only to awareness in the Renaissance. Therefore, the more convincing reading is that it was a deliberate choice of refusal.

One point is that the size of the elements on a canvas was based on their importance, hence, the more important the bigger the element was painted, throwing the perspective off. This was also done for practical reasons, since common folks were mostly illiterate, so icons had to find a way to translate visual scale into grammar, what is known as hierarchy of scale.

And the most important argument for the absence of an "ideal" perspective is that an icon's whole purpose is not organized around a human viewpoint at all. The vanishing point is replaced by the divine as the organizing center, not the observer. This is the argument of theological refusal-of-naturalism.

Both moves refuse the same premise, that meaning should be organized around how a human eye actually sees the world. In the end, it doesn't seem to matter whether you are being watched or doing the watching. Some things were never built to settle the question in the first place. What remains is that the ambiguity may be the whole argument.
